Lecture 16-1

What is a trickle bed reactor?

Three-phase reactorsFixed bed or slurryFlow and heat removalDesign concerns

Lecture 16-1

A fixed bed of catalyst with gas and liquid flowing down through it

  1. The family of three-phase reactorssix ways to contact gas, liquid and solid catalyst
  2. Fixed bed or slurry?particle size against pore diffusion and separation
  3. The trickle bed and its variantsflow direction, heat removal, strengths and weaknesses

Many reactions need a gas, a liquid and a solid catalyst at once.

Three-phase reactors · the family

The catalyst is either packed still or suspended in the liquid

Redrawn after Levenspiel, Ch. 21, Fig. 21.1 (source slide 5).

Three-phase reactors · compare two · try it

The trickle bed wins on separation and plug flow, loses on heat transfer

Reactor 1

Reactor 2

More stars, better performance. Ranade et al., Table 2 (source slide 7).

Against the stirred slurry the trickle bed gains separation, attrition and plug flow and gives up heat and mass transfer.

Fixed bed or slurry?

Choose the fixed bed when plug flow matters and the catalyst can be large

Fixed bed (trickle bed)

Gas and liquid move close to plug flow, best at low gas rates. Plug flow beats mixed flow except at very high conversion.

Slurry

Very fine particles: no internal diffusion limit, but the catalyst must be separated from the liquid afterwards.

So the particle size decides. The next slide puts a number on it.

Fixed bed or slurry · particle size · try it

Big pellets cost effectiveness; tiny particles cost pressure drop

$$\eta=\frac{1}{\phi}\left[\frac{1}{\tanh 3\phi}-\frac{1}{3\phi}\right],\ \ \phi=\frac{d_p}{6}\sqrt{\frac{k}{D_e}}$$
$\eta$–
liquid $\Delta P/L$–

$\eta$
effectiveness factor of a sphere
–
$k$
first-order rate constant per pellet volume
s$^{-1}$
$D_e$
pore diffusivity, $10^{-9}$; liquid water, 5 kg/m²s, $\varepsilon=0.4$
m$^2$/s

With $k=10^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ a 3 mm pellet keeps $\eta\approx0.9$: the trickle bed’s territory. Raise $k$ and only fine slurry particles stay effective.

Packing the catalyst still and letting both fluids trickle down gives the trickle bed.

The trickle bed

Liquid trickles over a fixed bed; gas fills the rest of the voids

  • A solid–liquid–gas contactor run in the trickle-flow regime.
  • Low gas and liquid rates: gas is continuous, liquid is dispersed as films and rivulets.
  • Liquid flows down; gas flows with it (co-current) or against it.
  • Mostly continuous; sometimes semi-batch.

Variants · by flow direction

Co-current downflow is the usual choice; counter-current is limited by flooding

Co-current downflow

No flooding limit on the flow rates; the liquid spreads thinner and more evenly.

Counter-current

Gas rising against the liquid floods the bed at high rates, so throughput is capped.

Variants · by heat removal

Remove heat through a jacket, through tubes in the bed, or by quench between beds

These are the thermal cases of Lecture 10 (2–3 internal exchange, 5 quench). 16-9 applies them to industrial units.

The trickle bed · strengths and weaknesses

Simple at high pressure, but fragile when the liquid is badly spread

Advantages

  • Runs three-phase reactions
  • Low energy use: the solid is not suspended
  • Simple at high T and P
  • Little catalyst attrition

Disadvantages

  • Hot spots where solvent evaporates
  • Channeling wastes catalyst
  • Poor performance if liquid is unevenly spread
  • Hard to control and to scale up: it hangs on hydrodynamics

The trickle bed · where it fits

Very slow reactions in porous pellets, or very fast ones on a coated shell

Slow reaction, porous pellet

Pore diffusion never limits, so large pellets work, as the particle-size interactive showed.

Fast reaction, coated pellet

Active metal only in a thin outer shell on a nonporous core, so there are no pores to diffuse through.

Main users: hydrotreating of oil fractions, hydrogenations, some oxidations in water. Section 16-9 surveys them.

Why the design is hard · scales

What happens in one pore depends on how liquid flows through the whole bed

After Ranade et al., Fig. 5 (source slide 14).

Why the design is hard · concerns

Design is still largely empirical, so it climbs the scales one step at a time

  • Empirical design: model parameters fitted at one scale are often unreliable at the next.
  • One model per scale: adiabatic plug flow is the usual assumption.
  • Consecutive scale-up: lab → pilot → semi-commercial → full scale.
  • Hydrodynamic mock-up: a cold, full-scale section at design flows shows the flow pattern.

Decisions the designer makes

  • Model level; 1st order good enough? (16-7)
  • True $k$ and overall $\eta$ (16-6)
  • Gas velocity, hence diameter (16-3, 16-4)
  • Number of beds, pellet size and shape (16-2, 16-9)
  • Internals: support, distributors (16-2)

Section 16-1 · summary

A trickle bed: fixed catalyst, gas continuous, liquid trickling down

  • Of six three-phase contactors it gives the best plug flow and catalyst separation, the worst heat transfer.
  • It suits reactions that stay kinetically controlled in millimetre pellets.
  • Co-current downflow avoids flooding; heat goes out by jacket, tubes or quench.
  • Its weak point is the liquid: maldistribution makes hot spots and wastes catalyst.

Next: what is actually inside the vessel.

Lecture 16-2

What are the parts inside a trickle bed reactor?

Vessel and bedsDistributorsCatalyst shapesStructured packing

Lecture 16-2

Everything inside the shell exists to spread the liquid evenly over the catalyst

  1. The vessel, one bed or severalinlet, tray, inert balls, catalyst, support, collector, quench
  2. The gas–liquid distributorwhat it must do; the main types; the chimney tray
  3. Random packing: catalyst shapesshape sets the void fraction, and the void fraction sets the pressure drop
  4. Structured packing and monolithswhen a coated block beats loose pellets

Vessel · single bed · click a part

Feed is spread, trickles through inert and catalyst layers, then is collected

Click a part of the vessel

Each part does one job; all of them serve one goal: the same liquid flow through every square metre of catalyst.

Only the catalyst bed reacts. Every other part exists to make the flow through it uniform.

Vessel · what it looks like inside

Liquid runs down as films and rivulets; gas fills the rest of the voids

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • The same parts as the clickable section, now in 3-D.
  • Liquid follows preferred paths; between them some pellets stay dry (16-3, 16-5).
  • Gas is the continuous phase in the trickle regime.

Vessel · several beds in one shell

Long reactors are split into beds, with quench and redistribution between them

  • Support grid carries each bed so the next can be cooled.
  • Quench: cold gas or liquid enters a mixing box that evens out temperature.
  • Redistribution tray re-spreads the liquid, which gathers at the wall as it flows down.
  • From a single stream, flow becomes even only after a bed depth of about 5 vessel diameters (Baker et al.).

The tray at the top decides how well the whole bed is used.

Distributor · requirements

A good tray spreads liquid evenly across the full range of flows

  • Low pressure drop
  • Works over a broad range of gas and liquid rates
  • Resists blocking and fouling
  • Easy to operate, install and clean
A tray that is slightly off level in a 4 m vessel starves one side of liquid: the dry side runs hot (16-3).

Distributor · types

Gravity trays let liquid fall through holes; vapour-assisted trays let the gas carry it

Weir channelliquid overflows notched troughs
Nozzlepressurised liquid through spray heads
Showerone spray cone over the bed
Sieve trayliquid drips through many holes
Sieve tray + gas chimneysgas bypasses through raised pipes
Downcomer tubeliquid enters notched pipes
Bubble capgas lifts liquid under a cap
Vapour liftgas drags liquid up a short leg, then down a long one

After Ranade et al., Ch. 2 (source slide 23): types a–h.

Distributor · short tube, slotted chimney

Liquid pools on the tray and enters each chimney through side slots

  • Liquid builds a level on the tray, so every chimney gets the same head.
  • Gas enters the cap above; liquid enters the slots below the level.
  • A higher flow raises the level and wets more slot: the tray self-adjusts.

Distributor · in a real vessel

A plant tray carries hundreds of chimneys across the full diameter

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Bolted sections with a manway, so it fits through the vessel nozzle.
  • Even chimney spacing gives each part of the bed its share of liquid.
  • The tray must be level: a tilt sends more liquid to the low side.

Under the tray lies the random packing: the catalyst pellets.

Random packing · catalyst shapes

Lobed and hollow shapes open the bed and shorten the diffusion path

  • Solid volume fraction is usually above 0.4: void fraction $\varepsilon$ below 0.6.
  • Lobes and holes give a shorter diffusion path for the same strength.
  • They also raise $\varepsilon$, which cuts the pressure drop (next slide).

Random packing · real pellets

Real hydroprocessing pellets: 1.5 to 5 mm, porous, many shapes

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Pellets standing on end show the cross-section.
  • Lobes and holes: shorter diffusion path, more voids.
  • Same order as the end-view sketch on the previous slide.

Random packing · void fraction · try it

A few more percent of voids lowers the pressure drop a lot

Ergun, one phase (Lecture 15)$\dfrac{\Delta P}{L}=Re\,(150+1.75\,Re)\left(\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{3}\dfrac{\mu^2}{\rho\,d_p^3}$
$\Delta P/L$–
vs. sphere bed–

Liquid alone, 5 kg/m²s water, $d_p=1.6$ mm. $\varepsilon$ from the source table (slide 44).

Going from spheres ($\varepsilon\approx0.39$) to quadrilobes ($0.59$) cuts the pressure drop about seven-fold at the same size.

Instead of loose pellets, the catalyst can be fixed onto an ordered structure.

Structured packing

Ordered channels a few millimetres wide replace the random voids

  • Monolith: ceramic or metal block of parallel channels, catalyst coated on the walls.
  • Static mixer: crimped plates, channels at an angle, alternate layers turned 90°, catalyst between plates.
  • Screen rolled in a coil: e.g. activated carbon bonded to the wires.

Structured packing · monolith

A monolith is one ceramic block of straight parallel channels

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Channels about 1 mm wide, walls coated with a thin catalyst washcoat.
  • Straight channels: low pressure drop, no pore diffusion deep in a pellet.
  • The cut block shows the channels run the full length.

Structured packing · monolith against random pellets

A monolith trades flexibility for low pressure drop and no pore diffusion

MonolithTrickle bed (pellets)
Pressure droplow, straight channelshigh with small pellets
Pore diffusionthin coat, little limitcan limit in mm pellets
Mass transfer, plug flowhigh; near plug flowmoderate
Liquid distributionno lateral mixing: inlet must be perfectbed re-spreads liquid
Changing the catalystreplace the whole blockdump and reload

Uses: H₂O₂ via a Pd-coated monolith; enzymes and cell culture (slide 27; Ranade Ch. 6).

Section 16-2 · summary

The internals exist to put the same liquid on every pellet

  • Tray, ceramic balls, support and collector make the flow uniform; only the bed reacts.
  • Long reactors are split into beds with quench and redistribution between them.
  • Lobed and hollow pellets raise $\varepsilon$: lower $\Delta P$ and a shorter diffusion path.
  • A monolith gives low $\Delta P$ and thin coats, but needs a perfect inlet distribution.

Next: how gas and liquid actually move through those voids.

16-3

Lecture 16-3

How do gas and liquid flow through the bed?

Inside the voidsFlow regimesFlow mapMaldistribution and hot spots

Lecture 16-3

The flow pattern decides how much catalyst works and how safely

  1. What happens in the voidsfilms, dry zones, stagnant pockets; why hydrodynamics controls the rest
  2. The flow regimestrickle, spray, pulse and bubble flow
  3. Reading the flow mapgas and liquid loadings, corrected for fluid properties
  4. Maldistribution and hot spotsa starved zone heats up; commercial evidence

Inside the voids

Not every pellet is wet, and not every drop of liquid moves

  • Flowing film renews reactant on the wetted surface.
  • Dry zone: gas touches the catalyst directly.
  • Stagnant cavity: liquid held between pellets, slow to exchange.
  • How much of each depends on the gas and liquid rates: the hydrodynamics.

Inside the voids · why it matters

Hydrodynamics sets the transfer rates, the model and the safety of the bed

Hydrodynamics itselfwhich phase is continuous; flow regime; pressure drop; liquid holdup
Mass transfergas–liquid and liquid–solid coefficients; apparent rate constant; overall effectiveness
Heat transfer and mixingaxial and radial dispersion; which design model is adequate
Operating problemsgas or liquid maldistribution; hot spots in exothermic reactions

Conversion and energy use both follow from these four (source slide 30).

Raise the gas and liquid rates and the flow changes its whole character.

Flow regimes · the list

With gas continuous the liquid trickles or sprays; with liquid continuous, gas bubbles or pulses

PhasesContinuous phaseRegimes
Two (G/S or L/S)the one fluidlaminar, turbulent
Three (G/L/S)gastrickling: liquid in rivulets, drops, films · spray: liquid as drops · foam: with surfactants
Three (G/L/S)liquidbubble · pulsing (slug): alternately gas-rich and liquid-rich

Flow regimes · pictures

Four regimes, from low loads to high

Flow regimes · how they are mapped

Regime maps come from transparent cold-flow columns with air and water

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Water and air flows are set on rotameters; the regime is seen through the wall.
  • Pressure taps along the column give $\Delta P$ for 16-4.
  • Air–water data are why real fluids need $\lambda$ and $\psi$.

Flow map · try it

Liquid and gas loadings place the bed on the map; fluid properties move the point

$\lambda$–
$\psi$–

–

Air–water: plotted at $(L, G)$. Other fluids: at $(L\psi,\ G/\lambda)$.

Hot oil has low surface tension ($\psi\approx6$): the same loads sit much closer to pulsing than air–water.

Flow map · the coordinates

Two property factors shift a real fluid onto the air–water map

$$\lambda=\left[\frac{\rho_G}{\rho_{air}}\,\frac{\rho_L}{\rho_{water}}\right]^{1/2}\quad \psi=\frac{\sigma_w}{\sigma_L}\left[\frac{\mu_L}{\mu_w}\left(\frac{\rho_w}{\rho_L}\right)^{2}\right]^{1/3}$$

Charpentier–Favier map (source slide 34): $x=G/\lambda$, $y=\lambda\psi L/G$, so $L\psi$ and $G/\lambda$ are air–water equivalents.

Flow map · quick criteria (air–water)

Below 20 kg/m²s of liquid and 0.2 kg/m²s of gas the bed trickles

RegimeLiquid $L$, kg/m²sGas $G$, kg/m²s
Trickle$<20$$<0.20$
Spray$<20$$>0.30$
Pulsing or slug$>20$$>0.20$
Bubble$>40$$<0.10$

Gaps between bands are transitions; $d_p$, shape and column size also matter (slides 34–35).

Even inside the trickle regime, the liquid rarely spreads evenly.

Maldistribution · sources inside the bed

Liquid prefers rivulets; packing defects make dry and stagnant regions

Filmcovers whole pellets: best wetting
Rivuletnarrow streams: pellets between stay dry
Drophangs and falls from pellet to pellet
Stagnant liquidheld at contact points
  • Bridges in the packing leave large voids.
  • Tight packing is poorly irrigated.
  • Tight packing around a trapped void makes a stagnant pocket.

Maldistribution · close up

Up close: some pellets carry a liquid film, their neighbours stay dry

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Glossy pellets: wetted, the liquid reactant reaches them.
  • Matte pellets: dry, gas touches the surface directly.
  • Liquid bridges hold at the contact points between pellets.

Maldistribution · hot spot · try it

Where less liquid flows, the same heat raises the temperature more

$$\Delta T_{zone}=\frac{\Delta T_{avg}}{m},\qquad m=\frac{L_{zone}}{L_{avg}}$$

Assumes the liquid carries the heat and the catalyst releases the same heat everywhere. Halving the local liquid doubles the local rise; past boiling the zone dries and runs away.

Maldistribution · at commercial scale

Stages and redistribution help, yet local hot spots still form

  • Commercial beds: 1–4 m diameter, 4–6 m long, in 3–4 stages.
  • Between stages: intermediate cooling and liquid redistribution.
  • Still, liquid flow differs from region to region; low-flow regions heat up.

Schematic only, after Jaffe (1976) in Ranade et al. (source slide 39): hydrocracker thermowell profiles.

Maldistribution · the evidence

The peaks do not follow the interstage coolers, so the cause is liquid maldistribution

  • Sharp temperature peaks along the bed mean hot spots that can overheat and damage the catalyst.
  • The peaks appear wherever the cooling is placed.
  • So cooling cannot be the cause: the most likely one is local liquid maldistribution.

The flow pattern is set. Next we put numbers on what it costs: the pressure drop.

Section 16-3 · summary

Stay in the trickle regime, and spread the liquid evenly

  • Pellets carry flowing films, dry zones and stagnant pockets; the rates decide the mix.
  • Trickle flow: roughly $L<20$ and $G<0.2$ kg/m²s for air–water.
  • Correct real fluids with $\lambda$ and $\psi$: hot oils sit closer to pulsing.
  • A starved zone has a rise of $\Delta T_{avg}/m$: maldistribution makes hot spots.

Lecture 16-4

How large is the pressure drop in a trickle bed?

Why it mattersEach phase aloneLockhart–MartinelliScale effects

Lecture 16-4

Compute each phase alone with Ergun, then combine the two

  1. Why the pressure drop mattersgas solubility, compressor duty, the rate itself
  2. Each phase flowing aloneErgun for the gas and for the liquid
  3. Combining them: Lockhart–Martinellithe parameter $\chi$; charts and the Larkins correlation
  4. What changes with scalepellet size, void fraction, the wall

Pressure drop · why it matters

Lower pressure down the bed means less dissolved gas, so a slower rate

  • Pressure falls along the bed because of friction and mole changes by reaction.
  • Less pressure, less gas dissolves: a gas-limited reaction slows.
  • Funk et al. (1990): rate rises with liquid flow, then falls once $\Delta P$ grows large.

Pressure drop · definitions

The two-phase drop is built from the drops of each phase flowing alone

$\Delta P$

The liquid falls by gravity, but the gas drags it and squeezes its path: two phases together lose more than the sum of each alone.

Each phase alone · Ergun

Use the same Ergun equation for the gas and for the liquid, each as if alone

$$\left(\frac{\Delta P}{L}\right)_{\!i}=Re_i\,(150+1.75\,Re_i)\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{3}\frac{\mu_i^2}{\rho_i\,d_p^3}$$
$$Re_G=\frac{G\,d_p}{\mu_G(1-\varepsilon)},\qquad Re_L=\frac{L\,d_p}{\mu_L(1-\varepsilon)}$$

$i=G$ or $L$. The 150 term is viscous loss, the 1.75 term inertial loss (Lecture 15).

Each phase alone · try it

The liquid usually loses more pressure than the gas, so $\chi>1$

$(\Delta P/L)_L$–

$\chi$–

Liquid is a thousand times denser: even small $L$ gives the larger drop. The bars split each drop into its viscous and inertial parts.

Now combine the two single-phase drops into one two-phase drop.

Two phases · Lockhart–Martinelli

The ratio of the two single-phase drops, $\chi$, sets the two-phase multiplier

$$\chi=\left[\frac{(\Delta P/L)_L}{(\Delta P/L)_G}\right]^{1/2}\qquad \left(\frac{\Delta P}{L}\right)_{LG}=\phi_L^2\left(\frac{\Delta P}{L}\right)_{L}$$
  • Read $\phi_L$ from a chart at $\chi$; co-current downflow.
  • Low-range chart: one curve per liquid flux $L$; liquid boiling point below 450 °C.
  • Heavier liquids (above 450 °C): chart by API gravity.
$\chi$
Lockhart–Martinelli parameter
–
$\phi_L$
two-phase multiplier on the liquid drop
–
$(\Delta P/L)_{LG}$
two-phase drop per metre
Pa/m

Charts in the source, slides 47–49.

Two phases · one equation for the charts

Larkins et al. fit the two-phase drop to $\chi$ alone

$$\log_{10}\frac{\Delta P_{LG}}{\Delta P_L+\Delta P_G}=\frac{0.416}{(\log_{10}\chi)^2+0.666}$$

Larkins, White and Jeffrey (1961), $0.05<\chi<30$. In Gas–Liquid–Solid Reactor Design, Eq. 6-8, and Hill, Eq. 8-224.

  • The ratio peaks at 4.2 when $\chi=1$: equal drops interact most.
  • Far from $\chi=1$ one phase dominates and the ratio falls toward 1.
  • A chart read and this fit can differ by tens of percent (Problem 16.5).

Two phases · try it

Two phases together lose up to four times the sum of each alone

Larkins$\log_{10}\dfrac{\Delta P_{LG}}{\Delta P_L+\Delta P_G}=\dfrac{0.416}{(\log_{10}\chi)^2+0.666}$
$\chi$–
$\Delta P_{LG}$–
$\phi_L^2$–

Default: $\Delta P_L=120$, $\Delta P_G=20$ Pa, as in Problem 16.5. Larkins gives about 450 Pa; check it against the chart reading there.

The same correlations behave very differently in a lab tube and a plant vessel.

Scale effects · pellets and voids

Negligible in the lab, large in the plant: size the pellets for both

  • Lab beds: short and porous ($\varepsilon\approx0.5$), so $\Delta P/L$ is negligible.
  • Commercial beds: $\Delta P$ is large; the pressure along the bed must enter the scale-up.
  • No pore diffusion limit? Use larger pellets and cut $\Delta P$.

From Ergun

$\Delta P/L$ falls steeply as $\varepsilon$ rises. In the viscous range $\Delta P/L\propto 1/d_p^2$; in the inertial range $\propto 1/d_p$.

Scale effects · the wall

In narrow lab tubes the wall loosens the packing; in plant vessels it does not

  • For $d_t/d_p<5$, porosity near the wall varies strongly.
  • On scale-up $d_p$ changes 1–5 times; the reactor diameter 20–100 times.
  • So large vessels see little wall effect, and a lower average porosity, about 0.4.
A lab tube with a loose wall layer has extra voids: more bypass, lower $\Delta P$ than the plant bed (16-8).

Section 16-4 · summary

Ergun for each phase, Lockhart–Martinelli to combine

  • Compute $\Delta P_L$ and $\Delta P_G$ with Ergun, each phase alone.
  • $\chi=\sqrt{\Delta P_L/\Delta P_G}$; then $\Delta P_{LG}=\phi_L^2\Delta P_L$ from a chart or Larkins.
  • The two-phase drop is up to about 4 times the sum of the parts.
  • Lab $\Delta P$ is negligible; plant $\Delta P$ lowers gas solubility and must enter the design.

Holdup · why it matters

The liquid in the bed stores heat and wets the catalyst

Safety

In a highly exothermic downflow bed, the holdup is the heat sink: know it to avoid hot spots and runaway.

Rate and selectivity

Holdup sets how much outer surface is wetted, and so whether reaction runs on wetted or dry catalyst.

Holdup · definitions

Split the bed volume into solid, gas, flowing liquid and stagnant liquid

$\varepsilon_B$
bed void fraction: voids / bed volume
–
$\varepsilon_G$, $\varepsilon_L$
gas, liquid holdup: volume / bed volume
–
$\beta_G$, $\beta_L$
saturation: volume / void volume
–

$\varepsilon_G+\varepsilon_L=\varepsilon_B$ and $\beta_i=\varepsilon_i/\varepsilon_B$. Liquid holdup counts flowing and stagnant liquid.

Holdup can be measured without opening the bed: inject a tracer and time it.

The stagnant liquid of Example 16.1 is one of several kinds of holdup.

Holdup · kinds

Holdup is split inside or outside the pellet, and draining or held

Where it is

  • Internal: liquid filling the catalyst pores
  • External: liquid outside the pellets

Whether it drains

  • Dynamic (free-draining): measured by stopping the flow; grows with liquid rate
  • Static (residual): by weighing or evaporation; independent of the flow rates

Tracer experiments can measure both (source slides 58–59).

Holdup · what moves it

More liquid flow raises holdup; more gas flow lowers it

Raises liquid holdup

higher liquid velocity, liquid viscosity, particle size; lower gas density at low gas rates

Lowers liquid holdup

higher gas velocity, higher gas density, higher surface tension

Measured trends: holdup 0.08–0.15 rising with $U_L$ (source slide 60); summary in Önsan & Avci, Ch. 5.

Holdup · correlation · try it

Liquid saturation follows the same $\chi$ as the pressure drop

$$\beta_t=\frac{a\,\chi^{b}}{1+a\,\chi^{b}}$$
curve$a$$b$range of $\chi$
10.660.810.1–80
20.920.300.05–100
34.830.58–
curve 1–
curve 2–
curve 3–

Morsi et al. (1982), Ranade Eq. 24. $\beta_t$: fraction of the voids (source labels it $\varepsilon_L$).

At $\chi=2.45$ (Problem 16.5) the three fits give $\beta_t$ from 0.55 to 0.89: the liquid system matters as much as $\chi$.

Holdup says how much liquid is there; wetting says how much catalyst it touches.

Wetting · definition

Wetting efficiency is the fraction of the pellets’ outer surface covered by flowing liquid

  • $\eta_{CE}$: external contacting efficiency (CE), 0 to 1.
  • Pores fill by capillarity even when the outside is part dry (except heavy oils).
  • Partial wetting is unique to trickle beds: other three-phase reactors keep pellets submerged.

Wetting · correlation · try it

Wetting rises with liquid flow and falls with pellet size

$$\eta_{CE}=1.617\,Re_L^{0.146}\,Ga_L^{-0.0711}$$
$Re_L$
$L\,d_p/\mu_L$
–
$Ga_L$
$d_p^3\rho_L^2g/\mu_L^2$, Galileo number
–
$Re_L$–
$Ga_L$–
$\eta_{CE}$–

El-Hisnawi, Duduković and Mills (1982), in Ranade Eq. 32; capped at 1. Bench loads ($L\sim0.1$) wet half the surface; plant loads wet nearly all.

Wetting · effect on the rate

Partial wetting helps a gas-limited reaction and hurts a liquid-limited one

Gas reactant limits

Gas reaches the dry surface directly, skipping the liquid film: the rate can rise. Example: fast noble-metal hydrogenations.

Non-volatile liquid reactant limits

Dry surface gets no reactant: the rate falls with $\eta_{CE}$. Example: hydrotreating, H₂ in excess (16-9).

Industrial hydroprocessors reach full use above about 7 kg/m²s; pilot plants at 0.07–0.7 kg/m²s do not (Ancheyta, Ch. 2).

Section 16-5 · summary

Holdup from tracers or $\chi$; wetting from the liquid flow

  • $V=v\,\bar t$ for each phase; the voids the tracer misses hold stagnant liquid.
  • Liquid saturation $\beta_t$ grows with $\chi$; the fit depends on the liquid.
  • $\eta_{CE}$ rises with $Re_L$; bench reactors are often half wetted.
  • Partial wetting raises gas-limited rates and lowers liquid-limited ones.

16-6

Lecture 16-6

What sets the apparent rate in a trickle bed?

Where it reactsResistances in seriesExample 16.2Operating variables

Lecture 16-6

Gas must dissolve, cross two films and enter a pore before it reacts

  1. Where the reaction happensthe phase of the product; the concentration profile
  2. Resistances in seriesderive the apparent rate for gas or liquid limiting
  3. Example 16.2: which step controls?hydrogenation of acetone, solved step by step
  4. Operating variablesgas and liquid velocity, temperature and pressure

Where it reacts

The reaction usually runs in the phase that carries the product

Liquid product

Reaction in the liquid: the gas must first dissolve. Most hydrogenations and hydrotreating.

Gas product

Reaction in the gas, on dry or thinly wetted catalyst.

$$A(g)+B(l)\xrightarrow{\ \text{solid catalyst}\ }\text{product}(l)$$

Resistances in series · the profile

Gas A falls through four steps on its way to the active site

  • Interface: equilibrium, $C_{Agi}=K_{gL}\,C_{Ali}$, like Henry’s law.
  • Then the liquid film, the liquid–solid film, and diffusion with reaction in the pellet.
  • B, in the liquid, crosses only the last two.

Resistances in series · symbols

One coefficient, and one area, for each step

$K_{gL}$
gas–liquid equilibrium constant, $C_{Agi}/C_{Ali}$
–
$k_ga_i$, $k_la_i$
gas-film, liquid-film coefficient × G–L area per reactor volume
s$^{-1}$
$k_ca_c$
liquid–solid coefficient × pellet area per mass of catalyst
m³/kg·s
$\eta$, $k_r'$
effectiveness factor; rate constant per mass of catalyst
–; m⁶/mol·kg·s
$(1-\varepsilon)\rho_p$
bed density $\rho_B$: catalyst mass per reactor volume
kg/m³

At steady state the same flux of A passes every step.

Resistances in series, derived · step 1 of 2

Write each step as a driving force, $r'$ per mass of catalyst

$\rho_Br'=k_ga_i\,(C_{Agb}-C_{Agi})$
gas film; per reactor volume
$\rho_Br'=k_la_i\,(C_{Ali}-C_{Alb}),\quad C_{Ali}=C_{Agi}/K_{gL}$
liquid film; interface equilibrium
$r'=k_ca_c\,(C_{Alb}-C_{As})$
liquid–solid film; per mass
$r'=\eta\,k_r'\,C_{As}\,C_{Bs}$
pore diffusion and reaction

Resistances in series, derived · step 2 of 2

Add the four drops; the interface concentrations cancel

$C_{Agb}-C_{Agi}=\dfrac{\rho_Br'}{k_ga_i},\quad C_{Agi}-K_{gL}C_{Alb}=\dfrac{K_{gL}\rho_Br'}{k_la_i}$
liquid film × $K_{gL}$
$K_{gL}(C_{Alb}-C_{As})=\dfrac{K_{gL}r'}{k_ca_c},\quad K_{gL}C_{As}=\dfrac{K_{gL}r'}{\eta k_r'C_{Bs}}$
last two × $K_{gL}$; then add all
$$r'=\frac{C_{Agb}}{\dfrac{K_{gL}}{\eta k_r'C_{Bs}}+\dfrac{(1-\varepsilon)\rho_p}{k_ga_i}+\dfrac{K_{gL}(1-\varepsilon)\rho_p}{k_la_i}+\dfrac{K_{gL}}{k_ca_c}}=k'_{app}\,C_{Agb}$$

Valid for A limiting, $C_B\gg C_A$, so $C_{Bs}=C_{Bb}$ (source slide 65).

Resistances in series · the other extreme

When the liquid reactant B limits, only the liquid–solid step and the pellet remain

$$r'=\frac{C_{Blb}}{\dfrac{1+K_AC_{As}+K_BC_{Bs}}{\eta k_r'C_{As}}+\dfrac{1}{k_{Bc}a_c}}\ \xrightarrow{\ 1\gg K_AC_{As}+K_BC_{Bs}\ }\ r'=k'_{app}\,C_{Blb}$$
  • $C_A\gg C_B$: dissolved A is the same everywhere, $C_{As}=C_{Ab}$.
  • $K_A$, $K_B$: adsorption constants of a Langmuir–Hinshelwood rate; small coverage gives first order in B.
  • Typical of hydrotreating: H₂ in large excess (source slide 66).

Resistances in series · try it

The largest of the four terms controls the rate

$$-r_A^{\,v}=\frac{C_{Agb}/K_{gL}}{R_{GL}+R_{LS}+R_{p}},\quad R=\frac{1}{\text{coefficient}}$$
$-r_A^{\,v}$, mol/m³s–

Per reactor volume: multiply $r'$ by $\rho_B$ and divide by $K_{gL}$. All terms in s; $C_{Agb}/K_{gL}=5.5$ mol/m³, pure gas so no gas film.

Now a full column: which step controls, and what conversion results?

Where do $k_ga_i$ and $k_la_i$ come from? From correlations, with care.

Correlations vary from system to system: use one fitted to your packing

With the rate equation in hand, we can ask what each operating variable does.

Operating variables · gas velocity

Gas velocity matters only when gas–liquid transfer controls

G–L transfer not controlling

Gas velocity has almost no effect on the rate.

G–L transfer controlling

Faster gas lowers liquid holdup and residence time, so conversion falls; but it can also raise $k_la_i$ (benzene hydrogenation, Metaxas & Papayannakos 2006).

Operating variables · liquid velocity · try it

Faster liquid wets more catalyst but stays a shorter time

$$X=1-\exp\!\left(-\frac{\eta_{CE}\,k_vH}{u_L}\right)$$
$k_v$
first-order constant, fully wetted, per bed volume
s$^{-1}$
$H$, $u_L$
bed height; liquid superficial velocity
m; m/s
$\eta_{CE}$–
LHSV–
$X$–

Liquid-limited, 1 m bed, 2 mm pellets, water. Rate per catalyst rises with $u_L$ (more wetted); conversion falls (shorter time): the trends of source slides 74–75.

Operating variables · temperature and pressure

Both usually raise the rate, but heat also evaporates the liquid

Higher temperature

  • Faster intrinsic rate; may raise gas solubility
  • Mass transfer can start to limit
  • More solvent vapour: lower partial pressure of the gas reactant, possibly a lower rate

Higher pressure

  • More gas reactant in both phases
  • Less solvent evaporates
  • Can mean a higher bed temperature in exothermic runs

Operating variables · temperature and wetting

Heat can dry the catalyst, with opposite results for volatile and non-volatile liquids

Volatile liquid

Evaporation dries part of the surface: gas–solid reaction starts there, fed by liquid held in the pores. With exothermic heat, multiple steady states can appear.

Non-volatile liquid

Less wetted surface means less liquid–solid contact: performance drops.

Section 16-6 · summary

Add the resistances; attack the largest

  • A limiting: four resistances, gas film, liquid film, liquid–solid, pellet; $r'=k'_{app}C_{Agb}$.
  • B limiting: only liquid–solid and pellet remain; $r'=k'_{app}C_{Blb}$.
  • Example 16.2: films take 75 % of the resistance; $X_B=0.41$.
  • Faster liquid: more wetting, shorter residence; temperature can dry the bed.

Model levels

Pseudo-homogeneous plug flow is the usual choice

ModelUse
Pseudo-homogeneous, plug flowusual choice

The equations · 1-D pseudo-homogeneous, plug flow

One mass and one energy balance along the bed

$$\big(\varepsilon_B+(1-\varepsilon_B)\varepsilon_p\big)\frac{\partial C_i}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial (uC_i)}{\partial z}+(1-\varepsilon_B)\rho_s\nu_ir'$$
$$\big(\varepsilon_B\rho_gC_{p,g}+(1-\varepsilon_B)\rho_sC_{p,s}\big)\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}=-G\,C_{p,g}\frac{\partial T}{\partial z}+(1-\varepsilon_B)\rho_s r'(-\Delta H_R)-\frac{4U}{d_T}(T-T_c)$$

$z$ along the flow. Source slide 80 prints $+\partial(uC_i)/\partial z$; with $z$ in the flow direction the convection term is negative.

bed voids; pellet porosity
–

The equations · with dispersion, 1-D and 2-D

Dispersion adds second-derivative terms, axial first, radial for wall-cooled beds

1-D plug flow, mass$\big(\varepsilon_B+(1-\varepsilon_B)\varepsilon_p\big)\partial_tC_i=-\partial_z(uC_i)+(1-\varepsilon_B)\rho_s\nu_ir'$
$+\ \varepsilon_BD_{ax}\dfrac{\partial^2C_i}{\partial z^2}$
axial dispersion; energy gains $+\lambda_{ax}\partial^2T/\partial z^2$
$+\ \varepsilon_BD_{rad}\left(\dfrac{\partial^2C_i}{\partial r^2}+\dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial C_i}{\partial r}\right)$
2-D: radial dispersion; energy gains $\lambda_{rad}$ terms

$D_{ax}$, $D_{rad}$: axial, radial dispersion coefficients (m²/s); $\lambda$: effective conductivities (W/m·K). Source slides 80–81.

Where do these extra terms come from physically?

Dispersion · mechanisms

Different path lengths spread the fluid along the bed; splitting flow spreads it sideways

Axial dispersion

  • Short and long flow paths; uneven axial velocity
  • Diffusion into porous pellets and stagnant pockets, so it depends on diffusivity
  • Usually negligible in deep beds

Radial dispersion

  • Bypass along the wall
  • Streamlines split and rejoin around pellets
  • Radial gradients from wall cooling drive a diffusive flux

Dispersion · radial, and what RTD tells us

2-D models are rare; the residence time distribution is the practical tool

  • Radial correlations are not well developed; 2-D models are rarely used.
  • Needed only for a non-adiabatic bed cooled through the wall.
  • Packed beds: $Pe_{ax}\approx2$, $Pe_{rad}\approx10$, so $D_{rad}\approx D_{ax}/5$.

Residence time distribution (RTD)

Industrial beds flow nearly in plug flow but mix locally. A tracer RTD reveals wetting, channeling, maldistribution and liquid mixing without seeing inside (Lectures 11–13).

Source slide 86 prints $D_{rad}=5D_{ax}$; the Peclet numbers above give the reverse.

When dispersion matters · the criterion

A bed is long enough when its length beats a limit set by $X$, $n$ and $Bo$

$$\frac{L}{d_p}>\frac{20\,n}{Bo}\ln\frac{1}{1-X}\qquad Bo=\frac{d_p\,u_L}{D_{ax}}$$
  • Mears (1971): liquid axial dispersion changes the needed length by less than 5 %.
  • Gierman (1988): replace 20 by 8 for about 1 °C of temperature error.
  • Liquid dispersion matters as much as wetting and holdup; gas dispersion much less.
$L$
bed length
m
$n$
reaction order (apparent)
–
$Bo$
Bodenstein (particle Péclet) number; about 0.04 in lab trickle beds
–
$D_{ax}$
liquid axial dispersion coefficient
m²/s

Source slide 84; Gierman form and Bo ≈ 0.04: Ancheyta, Ch. 2.

When dispersion matters · try it

High conversion and low $Bo$ demand a very long bed

Mears (20) / Gierman (8)$\dfrac{L}{d_p}>\dfrac{20\,n}{Bo}\ln\dfrac{1}{1-X}$
Mears $L/d_p$–
Gierman $L/d_p$–

Mears is the stricter rule. At lab $Bo\approx0.04$ and 95 % conversion even Gierman asks for $L/d_p$ near 900.

When dispersion matters · what it costs · try it

Below the criterion the dispersed bed falls short of plug flow

$$X=1-\frac{4a\,e^{Pe/2}}{(1+a)^2e^{aPe/2}-(1-a)^2e^{-aPe/2}},\ a=\sqrt{1+\frac{4Da}{Pe}}$$

$a$: shorthand; $Pe=Bo\,L/d_p$; $Da=k\tau$.

$Pe=Bo\,L/d_p$–
$X$ plug–
$X$ dispersed–

First order, Damköhler $Da=k\tau=3$ (plug $X=0.95$); $Pe$: bed Péclet; Wehner–Wilhelm (Lecture 12). Past $Pe\approx100$ the curves meet.

Apply the criterion to a real bench reactor.

EXAMPLE 16.3Is a bench hydrotreater long enough for plug flow?

A bench-scale trickle bed for diesel hydrodesulfurization holds a 0.30 m bed of 1.6 mm catalyst extrudates. The target sulfur conversion is 95 %, the apparent reaction order is 1.5, and the liquid Bodenstein number at bench flow is 0.04.

(a) Does the bed satisfy the Mears criterion? (b) The Gierman criterion? (c) The catalyst is diluted with 0.2 mm SiC fines, which then set the particle size. Check Gierman again.

Bed length $L$0.30 m
Catalyst $d_p$1.6 mm
Fines $d_p$0.2 mm
$X$0.95
$n$1.5
$Bo$0.04

Built for this lecture from the criteria in Ancheyta, Ch. 2.

Example 16.3 · solution

EXAMPLE 16.3Undiluted, the bed is far too short; fines make it pass Gierman

Criterion$\dfrac{L}{d_p}>\dfrac{c\,n}{Bo}\ln\dfrac{1}{1-X}$, $c=20$ Mears, $c=8$ Gierman
$\dfrac{n}{Bo}\ln\dfrac{1}{1-X}=\dfrac{1.5}{0.04}\ln 20=112.3$
common factor
(a) need $20\times112.3=2247$; have $0.30/0.0016=188$: fails
would need 3.6 m of bed
(b) need $8\times112.3=899$; have 188: fails
would need 1.4 m
(c) need 899; have $0.30/0.0002=1500$: passes
fines set $d_p$

Bed length is one half of the shape; diameter is the other.

Reactor aspect ratio

Tall beds run closer to plug flow; short beds need less pressure drop

High $L/D$ (tall)Low $L/D$ (short)
Velocities, transfer rateshigherlower
Flow pattern, wettingnear plug flow; better wettingmore back-mixing; lower wetting
Liquid distributionbetter radially; may need redistributionhard to make uniform
Heatjackets or interbed cooling possibleinternal coils; hot-spot risk if adiabatic
Pressure drophigher: limits pellet sizelower: larger pellets allowed

Commercial $L/D\approx0.5$–10; pilot and bench 5–100. Similar velocities at both scales are hard to keep (source slides 87–88).

Section 16-7 · summary

Plug flow first; prove dispersion negligible with the criterion

  • Usual model: 1-D pseudo-homogeneous plug flow, mass plus energy.
  • Add $D_{ax}$ for liquid dispersion; 2-D only for wall-cooled, large beds.
  • Check $L/d_p>(20n/Bo)\ln[1/(1-X)]$; at lab $Bo\approx0.04$ beds fail unless diluted with fines.
  • Tall beds approach plug flow at the price of pressure drop.

Lecture 16-8

How do we scale a trickle bed up, and down?

Scales and methodStep-by-step procedureSame LHSV, different flowScale-down

Lecture 16-8

Each size change needs data, because the hydrodynamics change with size

  1. The scales and the methodbench, pilot, commercial; seven linked activities
  2. The scale-up procedurelab, demonstration, pilot and mock-up, commercial
  3. Same LHSV, different hydrodynamicswhy lab and plant disagree at equal space velocity
  4. Scaling downbench reactors that still represent the plant

Scales · bench to commercial

The same catalyst, in beds from tens of centimetres to tens of metres

  • Commercial: about 16 m of bed, several beds, 1–4 m wide.
  • Pilot: 1–4 m long. Bench: 0.3–1 m. Micro: under 0.5 m.
  • The arrows run up-scale, but the knowledge also runs back down.

Scales · the method

Seven linked activities connect performance with hardware and operation

1 · Lab reactionskinetic data; wetting issues
2 · Effective ratepore and film resistances, kinetics
3 · Hydrodynamicsregime, $\Delta P$, holdup, wetting
4 · Preliminary designdiameter, aspect ratio, cooling
5 · Pilot and cold flowRTD, distribution, transfer
6 · Final designmodels validated, scale-up
7 · Resolve complexityCFD, distributors, evaporation
Loopseach step feeds back to the others

After Ranade et al., Ch. 5 (source slide 91).

Scales · why not design directly?

A trickle bed cannot be designed from correlations alone

A priori design is impossible

Mass transfer always matters, and it depends on regime, fluids, packing and loadings. The correlations are incomplete and unreliable.

So scale up each size change

Measure the apparent rate constant at one size; use it with a plug flow model to size the next.

Procedure · click through the stages

Measure $k_{app}$ at each scale; use it with plug flow to size the next

Laboratory (often a stirred tank)

  • Yield and conversion against $G$, $L$, $T$, $P$ and feed concentration, for the chosen catalyst.
  • Choose $T$, $P$ and feed concentration.
  • $k_{app}$ as a function of $G$ and $L$.

Demonstration size (pilot 1, a trickle bed)

  • Size it with the lab $k_{app}$ and plug flow; height and diameter from site and budget; $G$, $L$ for the output wanted.
  • Measure yield, $k_{app}$ against $G$, $L$; possibly holdup, $\Delta P$ and dispersion.

Pilot plant (pilot 2) and hydrodynamic mock-up

  • Catalyst, size, feed, $T$, $P$ and target now fixed: optimise $G$ and $L$.
  • Target: a half-scale model of the plant at plant operating conditions.
  • Mock-up: a cold section at design flows to watch wetting, $\Delta P$ and holdup.

Commercial plant

  • Diameter for the same $G$ and $L$ as the pilot; add heat transfer and redistribution; set bed depths.
  • Plug flow with the pilot $k_{app}$ gives the number of stages; check with higher models (holdup, $\Delta P$, dispersion).
  • In operation, measure $k_{app}$, holdup and $\Delta P$ to verify.

Scale-up · the bench unit

A bench trickle bed: a thin tube in a furnace, fed by a pump and flow controllers

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Tube about 1.5 cm wide, bed tens of centimetres long.
  • Three-zone furnace keeps the bed isothermal.
  • A back-pressure regulator holds the H₂ pressure; the product is sampled after a separator.

Why not simply keep the space velocity the same? The data say it fails.

Same LHSV · the evidence

At the same LHSV the plant hydrotreater converts 20–30 points more than the lab

  • Hydrotreating; 4 MPa (lab) and 4.4 MPa (plant); gas/liquid 200–300 m³/m³.
  • Same catalyst, same space velocity, different velocities and wetting.

Traced approximately from Gunjal and Ranade (2007), source slide 97.

The lab bed is short, so its liquid moves slowly: poor wetting and more dispersion. The next slide puts numbers on it.

Same LHSV · try it

At equal LHSV the liquid velocity scales with bed length

$$\text{LHSV}=\frac{Q_L}{V_{bed}}=\frac{u_L}{H}\ \Rightarrow\ u_L=\text{LHSV}\cdot H$$

LHSV: liquid volume flow per bed volume. Oil: 700 kg/m³, 0.3 mPa·s; $d_p=1.6$ mm.

The bench bed sees about 30 times less liquid flux: half-wetted catalyst. Diluting with fines (next) is the usual fix.

Same LHSV · typical values

Plants run at much higher throughputs than bench units

ParameterCommercialPilotBenchMicro
Liquid flux, kg/m²s2.5–250.8–60.08–0.250.03–0.09
Gas flux, kg/m²s0.4–40.01–10.01–0.080.0001–0.05
Wetting efficiency0.6–10.4–0.90.1–0.70.8–1
Liquid holdup0.16–0.250.1–0.20.05–0.140.15–0.25
Bed length, m161–40.3–10.008–0.5

Ranade et al., Ch. 5, Table 3 (source slides 98–99). Higher liquid flux raises holdup, wetting and transfer rates.

Turn the problem round: make a small reactor behave like the big one.

Scale-down · what limits it

A small bed must stay isothermal, in plug flow and fully wetted

What spoils a small bed

  • Loose packing at the wall
  • Deviation from plug flow
  • Poor irrigation of the pellets
  • Non-uniform catalyst sample; radial heat gradients

Four ways to scale down

  • Geometric similarity
  • A narrow column “cut out” of the plant bed (single-pellet string)
  • Fluid dynamic similarity
  • Phenomenological: match the controlling step

Önsan & Avci, Ch. 5, Sec. 5.4.2.

Scale-down · rules of thumb

Dilute with fines, and keep $L/d_p$ and $D/d_p$ large

$L/d_p$Purpose
>30–50neglect axial dispersion, simple rule
>100trickle beds
>350bench HDT of gas oil (Mears)
$D/d_p$Purpose
>10reduce wall effects
>16avoid wall flow (Gierman)
>20–25avoid wall bypass

Inert fines (e.g. SiC) raise wetting and set $d_p$ here. Ancheyta, Tables 2.3, 2.5.

Section 16-8 · summary

Scale step by step, and watch the liquid velocity

  • Correlations alone cannot size a trickle bed: measure $k_{app}$ at each scale.
  • Lab → demonstration → half-scale pilot and cold mock-up → plant at the same $G$ and $L$.
  • Same LHSV means $u_L\propto H$: a short bench bed is under-wetted and more dispersed.
  • Fines dilution and large $L/d_p$, $D/d_p$ make a bench bed representative.

Lecture 10 framework · geometry and catalyst life

Three phases with a solid catalyst: slurry, trickle bed, or fluidised slurry

PhasesTypical geometry
1 (L or G)stirred tank; tube
2 (incl. S cat–G)columns, slurry tanks, fixed / fluidised / moving beds
3: S cat–L–Gslurry, trickle bed, fluidised slurry, air-lift
4: S–L–L–Gmulti-impeller slurry tank

Catalyst life picks the bed

  • Small $k'$, slow deactivation, life of months–years: a fixed bed, so a trickle bed.
  • Fast deactivation: moving or fluidised bed, e.g. moving-bed (OCR) hydrodesulfurisation of residue.

Lecture 10-2 (after Ray & Das, 2020).

Lecture 10 framework · heat management

Of the six thermal cases, trickle beds mostly use 1, 4 and 5

CaseStrategyTrickle bed use
1adiabatic single bedmild hydrogenations
2–3internal exchange: jacket, coils, tubessmall or basket units (16-1)
4adiabatic beds in series, interstage coolinghydrocracking trains
5external mass: cold shots, recycle, diluenthydroprocessing quench (H₂ or liquid)
6multitubularrare for trickle flow: distribution to every tube is hard

Cases from Lecture 10-4; examples from Lecture 10 and Ancheyta, Ch. 3.

With the framework set, survey where trickle beds actually run.

Industrial examples · click a process

From 1 MPa hydrogenations to 20 MPa residue hydrotreating

Hydroprocessing needs the highest pressures; hydrogenations of fine chemicals run cooler and lower. Every one is three-phase with a long-lived catalyst.

P, T: source slides 12–13 (Ranade, Table 1); HDT (hydrotreating): Ancheyta, Table 3.1.

Industrial examples · what limits each family

Hydroprocessing is liquid-limited; noble-metal hydrogenations are gas-limited

FamilyWhat limitsDesign worry
Hydroprocessing (HDS, HDN, HDM)bulky S, N molecules in the liquid; H₂ in excesswetting, long beds, quench
Hydrogenation on noble metalsfast, exothermic: gas–liquid transferhot spots, multiple steady states
Fine chemicalsthermal stability of the productprecise temperature control
Oxidation in waterO₂ solubilitygas–liquid transfer, pressure

Ranade et al., Ch. 6. Partial wetting cuts the first family’s rate and can raise the second’s (16-5).

The largest trickle beds in the world are hydrotreaters. Look at one closely.

Hydrotreater · what it does

Hydrogen removes S, N, O and metals; heavier feeds need harsher conditions

  • HDS sulfur, HDN nitrogen, HDO oxygen removal
  • HDA aromatics saturation, HDM metals (V, Ni), HDAs asphaltenes
  • HDC: some cracking to lighter products

Severity follows the feed

Naphtha and straight-run distillates carry fewer, easier impurities; vacuum gas oil and residue carry more, plus metals and polynuclear aromatics (PNA). Higher boiling point, higher severity.

Ancheyta, Sec. 3.1.

Hydrotreater · the unit

The reactor is one item in a unit built around hydrogen recycle

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Heater and feed–effluent exchangers bring the feed to inlet temperature.
  • The high-pressure separator splits product oil from H₂-rich gas.
  • An amine scrubber removes H₂S; the compressor recycles the H₂.

Hydrotreater · reactor types

Fixed beds for light feeds; moving, ebullated or slurry beds when the catalyst dies fast

Fixed bed (trickle)most common, simple; light feeds, now also residue; catalyst life months–years
Moving bed (OCR)catalyst added and withdrawn on stream; residue with high metals
Ebullated bedcatalyst expanded by recycled oil; near well mixed; difficult feeds
Slurry bedfine catalyst carried with the oil; leaves with the residue

Naphtha HDS is two-phase (fully vaporised); heavier feeds trickle (Ancheyta, 3.1.1).

Hydrotreater · operating window

Heavier feed: higher pressure, lower space velocity, more hydrogen

Feed$T$, °C$P$, psig (MPa)LHSV, h$^{-1}$H₂ use, scf/bbl
Naphtha280–425200–800 (1.4–5.5)1.5–5.0100–700
Gas oil340–425800–1600 (5.5–11)0.5–1.5300–800
Residue340–4502000–3000 (13.8–20.7)0.2–1.0500–2000

Ancheyta, Table 3.1. Four levers: H₂ partial pressure, temperature, H₂/oil ratio, space velocity.

Hydrotreater · internals

Two or more beds, each with its tray, balls, support and a quench zone below

  • Inlet distributor tray → ceramic balls → catalyst → support.
  • Quench box: cold H₂ (or liquid) mixes with the hot stream.
  • Redistributor tray re-spreads the liquid over bed 2.
  • Outlet collector under the last bed (Ancheyta, Fig. 3.2; 16-2).

Hydrotreater · internals in 3-D

Two beds with a quench zone between them

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • Cold H₂ enters through the ring; the mixing box evens out the temperature.
  • The redistribution tray spreads the liquid again over bed 2.
  • Thermocouples at several heights track each bed’s rise.

Hydrotreater · three phases and the rate

H₂ dissolves, sulfur compounds react on the catalyst, H₂S inhibits

$$r_{HDS}=k_{HDS}\,\frac{C_S^{\,S}\,(C_{H_2}^{\,S})^{0.45}}{\big(1+K_{H_2S}\,C_{H_2S}^{\,S}\big)^2}$$

Langmuir–Hinshelwood form, superscript $S$ = at the catalyst surface; $E_A=132$ kJ/mol, $\Delta H_R=-251$ kJ/mol (Ancheyta, Table 3.6).

  • Gas-film resistance is usually neglected; H₂ at the interface is in equilibrium with its partial pressure.
  • H₂S and NH₃ go back to the gas; H₂S adsorbs and slows HDS (squared term).
  • The surface sulfur concentration follows the liquid film and $\eta$: the B-limiting case of 16-6.

Heat and operation · quench design · try it

Splitting the bed and quenching keeps every bed below the temperature limit

rise per bed–
peak $T$–
quench zones–

Equal conversion per bed and quench back to the inlet temperature assumed; limit 425 °C, the top of the gas-oil window. Lecture 10 Case 5 in action.

Heat and operation · hydrogen or liquid quench?

Hydrogen quench helps the reaction; liquid quench carries more heat

Hydrogen

  • replenishes H₂; dilutes H₂S and NH₃; less coke
  • faster gas helps the redistributor tray
  • low heat capacity; more recycle compression
  • more pressure drop; taller reactor

Liquid (product or feed)

  • high heat capacity; less equipment
  • second pass for unreacted species
  • raises LHSV: less severity
  • if it vaporises, H₂ partial pressure falls

Ancheyta, Table 3.2.

Heat and operation · what goes wrong

Over months the top of the bed becomes a filter and the pressure drop climbs

Clogging

Fine solids at about 100 wt ppm in heavy gas oil collect in the bed. The bed turns into a filter; $\Delta P$ rises until the unit stops to change catalyst (Önsan & Avci, 5.5.1).

Hot spots and scale-up

Poor distribution makes hot spots (16-3). Pilot HDT units at the plant LHSV are under-wetted (16-8): dilute with fines and check Mears (Example 16.3).

Heat and operation · at shutdown

At shutdown the top of the bed is a crust of fines, scale and coke

AI-generated illustration (Gemini)

  • The crust traps solids from the feed: the bed acts as a filter.
  • Its pressure drop climbs until the unit stops to skim or change catalyst.
  • Graded balls and guard rings on top delay it.

Section 16-9 · summary

Long-lived catalyst, three phases, quench between beds: the hydrotreater

  • Lecture 10 logic: three phases and a long catalyst life give a fixed trickle bed.
  • Trickle beds run from 0.1 to about 20 MPa: hydroprocessing, hydrogenations, oxidations.
  • HDT is liquid-limited; H₂S inhibits; heat is managed with quench (Case 5).
  • Watch distribution, clogging and wetting at pilot scale.

Choosing the reactorModelsPressure drop and regimeHydrotreating

Class Activity

Ten problems in four groups: read the statement, decide, then turn the page

  1. Choosing the reactor: 16.1, 16.2, 16.8why three phases; slurry or trickle bed (16-1, 16-5)
  2. Hydrodynamics: 16.5, 16.6, 16.7two-phase pressure drop, flow regime, a pilot unit (16-3 to 16-6)
  3. Models and rates: 16.3, 16.4, 16.9which model level; the HDS rate (16-6, 16-7)
  4. Hydrotreater design: 16.10number of beds and the quench fluid (16-9)

Problem 16.1 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.1Why use a three-phase reactor?

Three phase reactor is employed because

(a) it gives higher rates of reaction.
(b) one of the reactant can not be vaporized.
(c) the heat transfer rate is higher than a liquid phase reactor.
(d) small catalyst particle can be used.

Source slide 101.

Problem 16.1 · solution

PROBLEM 16.1Answer (b): one reactant stays liquid while the other is a gas

  • (b) A heavy or heat-sensitive reactant cannot be vaporised, so the gas must dissolve into it: three phases are unavoidable.
  • (a) No: the extra gas–liquid step usually makes the rate lower than a gas-phase reaction (16-6).
  • (c) No: trickle beds have the poorest heat transfer of the multiphase reactors (16-1).
  • (d) Small particles suit a slurry, but they are a consequence of the choice, not the reason for three phases.

Problem 16.2 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.2A reactor for a slow fatty-ester hydrogenation

Given that the hydrogenation of a fatty ester is catalyzed in the liquid phase by a dispersed Raney Nickle catalyst with fine particles and is slow so that a long contact time is needed, the reactor you would recommend for this hydrogenation is

a) a gas phase, tubular reactor with the Raney Nickle agglomerated into large pellets that are packed into the reactor.
b) a co-current down flow trickle bed reactor bed with the Raney Nickle agglomerated into large pellets that are packed into the reactor.
c) a counter-current, liquid down flow, hydrogen upflow trickle bed reactor bed with the Raney Nickle agglomerated into large pellets that are packed into the reactor.
d) a mechanically stirred slurry reactor with a gas sparger to feed hydrogen in which the Raney Nickle catalyst is added along with the fatty ester and continually removed in the over flow of the liquid phase from the reactor.

Source slide 102.

Problem 16.2 · solution

PROBLEM 16.2Answer (d): a stirred slurry, because the catalyst is already a fine powder

  • (d) A slurry holds a large liquid volume for the long contact time, uses the fine powder as it is, and carries it out with the overflow.
  • (a) No: a fatty ester does not vaporise; this is a liquid-phase reaction.
  • (b), (c) A trickle bed would need a very long bed or a very low liquid flow for that contact time: poor wetting (16-5), and Raney nickel pellets are weak.

Problem 16.3 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.3Why are heterogeneous models rarely used?

Heterogeneous dispersion or plug flow models are rarely used for analyzing trickle bed data or sizing trickle beds reactor because

a) these models oversimplify transport and mixing processes in trickle beds
b) these models neglect internal diffusion in catalyst particles or immobilized enzyme supports
c) temperature differences between particles and flowing fluids are negligible.
d) these models contain too many parameters that are difficult to determine accurately

Source slide 103.

Problem 16.3 · solution

PROBLEM 16.3Answer (d): too many uncertain parameters

  • (d) Separate gas, liquid and solid balances need $k_ga_i$, $k_la_i$, $k_ca_c$, wetting and dispersion, each uncertain by tens of percent (16-6, 16-7).
  • (a) No: they are the most detailed models, not oversimplified.
  • (b) No: heterogeneous models are exactly the ones that include internal diffusion.
  • (c) That is a reason a pseudo-homogeneous model may suffice, not why heterogeneous ones are avoided.

Problem 16.4 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.4When is 1-D plug flow enough?

Trickle bed models can be simplified to a 1-dimensional, pseudo homogeneous plug flow model if

a) the hydrodynamic flow regime is pulse flow and the reactor operates adiabatically
b) the reactor has a high aspect ratio (L/dp) and the heat of reaction is small regardless of hydrodynamic regime.
c) the reactor diameter is large and deep with poor radial mixing and operation in the trickle flow regime
d) the reactor operates in the trickle regime, but has a low aspect ratio and conversion is expected to be high.

Source slide 104.

Problem 16.4 · solution

PROBLEM 16.4Answer (b): a long bed and little heat

Mears$\dfrac{L}{d_p}>\dfrac{20\,n}{Bo}\ln\dfrac{1}{1-X}$
  • (b) High $L/d_p$ passes Mears, so axial dispersion drops out; little heat means no radial gradients, so 1-D works.
  • (c) Poor radial mixing in a large bed calls for a 2-D model.
  • (d) Low $L/d_p$ with high $X$ is exactly where Mears fails.
  • (a) The regime alone does not decide; nothing says dispersion is negligible.

Problem 16.5 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.5Two-phase pressure drop from the single-phase drops

Pressure drop in a trickle bed is usually estimated from the pressure drops exhibited by the gas and liquid phases as if each alone flowed through the bed. If the pressure drop for the liquid with flowrate 10 kg/(m²·s) is 120 Pa and the pressure drop for the gas is 20 Pa, the pressure drop for gas-liquid flow will be,

a. 100 Pa   b. 235 Pa   c. 535 Pa   d. 635 Pa   e. Can not be calculated because the particle diameter is not known.

Source slides 105–106.

Problem 16.5 · solution

PROBLEM 16.5Answer (d): $\chi=2.45$, chart $\phi_L=2.30$, so $\Delta P_{LG}\approx635$ Pa

Lockhart–Martinelli$\chi=\sqrt{\Delta P_L/\Delta P_G}$, $\Delta P_{LG}=\phi_L^2\,\Delta P_L$
$\chi=\sqrt{120/20}=2.45$
only the two single drops are needed, not $d_p$: (e) is wrong
low-range chart, $L\approx10$ kg/m²s curve: $\phi_L\approx2.30$
read at $\chi=2.45$
$\Delta P_{LG}=2.30^2\times120=635$ Pa
option (d)

Cross-check, Larkins: $3.23\times(120+20)=452$ Pa. Source slides mark “(C)” and list 335 or 535 Pa for (c); 635 Pa is (d).

Problem 16.5 · how sure is the answer? · try it

PROBLEM 16.5A small change in the chart reading moves the answer between options

Chart$\Delta P_{LG}=\phi_L^2\,\Delta P_L$, $\ \Delta P_L=120$ Pa
$\Delta P_{LG}$, chart–
Larkins–
nearest option–

$\phi_L$ from 2.1 to 2.4 spans 530–690 Pa: options (c) and (d) differ by less than the reading error of the chart.

Problem 16.6 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.6Which hydrodynamic regime?

What is the hydrodynamic regimes in the trickle bed reactor with 0.50 void fraction of bed. in the cold flow test using water and air. The liquid loading is 30 kg/(m²·s) and gas loading is at 0.25 kg/(m²·s).

(a) Trickle flow   (b) Pulse or slug flow   (c) Between bubble and pulse flow   (d) Bubble flow   (e) Can not specify, it depend on the scale of reactor

Source slide 110.

Problem 16.6 · solution

PROBLEM 16.6Answer (b): both loadings are past the pulsing limits

Air–water criteriapulse: $L>20$, $G>0.20$  ·  trickle: $L<20$, $G<0.20$  ·  bubble: $L>40$, $G<0.10$
  • $L=30>20$ and $G=0.25>0.20$: pulse or slug flow.
  • (a) needs $L<20$; (d) needs $L>40$, $G<0.10$.
  • (e) No: the regime is set by loadings and fluid properties, not by reactor size.
  • Variant (slide 108): $G=0.15$ is below 0.20 and $L=30$ is below 40, so the point sits in the transition, not a clean regime.

Problem 16.7 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.7A pilot-scale trickle bed hydrogenation

A pilot scale, trickle bed hydrogenation reactor, operating at 20 bar and 400°C, has a diameter of 1 m and uses a Pd/Al₂O₃ catalyst with an effective spherical diameter of 3 mm. The liquid loading is 5.0 kg/m² s, and the gas loading is 320 kg/m² s. The gas phase entering the reactor contains 80% hydrogen by volume. The diffusivity of hydrogen in the liquid phase is 2.4 x 10⁻⁹. The catalyst particles are fully wetted. Bed void fraction is 0.43 and the density of the catalyst particles is 1,450 kg/m³. The reaction is assumed first order.

(a) The reactor can be operated isothermally. (b) The rate of reaction depends on mass transfer coefficient of hydrogen from gas phase to liquid phase. (c) Diffusion of hydrogen dissolved in liquid phase through catalyst pore is the most important step. (d) Heat transfer from the catalyst particle is mostly responsible by liquid phase.

Source slide 112.

Problem 16.7 · solution

PROBLEM 16.7Answer (d): fully wetted pellets lose their heat to the liquid

  • (d) “Fully wetted” means only liquid touches the pellet surface: the liquid carries the heat away.
  • (a) A 1 m adiabatic bed with an exothermic hydrogenation is not isothermal.
  • (b) The gas is 80 % H₂: the gas-film resistance is negligible; any G–L resistance sits on the liquid side.
  • (c) No rate constant is given, so a Thiele modulus cannot show pore diffusion to be “the most important” step.

Gas loading 320 kg/m²s is far outside trickle flow; 0.32 is likely meant. No key in the source.

Problem 16.8 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.8Comparison of three-phase reactor systems

Comparison of three phase reactor systems.

(a) Hot spot problem sometimes occurs in trickle bed reactor and mechanically stirred slurry reactor.
(b) Liquid holdup in trickle bed reactor is always less than in mechanically stirred reactor.
(c) In highly exothermic reaction, liquid phase in trickle bed reactor can be evaporated.
(d) Pseudo-homogeneous models can be used to represent both reactors.

Source slide 113. Decide which statements are true.

Problem 16.8 · solution

PROBLEM 16.8(b) and (c) are true; (a) and (d) fail for the slurry

  • (b) A trickle bed holds 0.05–0.25 of its volume as liquid; a stirred slurry is mostly liquid (16-5).
  • (c) A starved, hot zone can boil off the liquid and dry the catalyst (16-3).
  • (a) A stirred slurry is well mixed: its temperature is uniform, so no hot spot.
  • (d) A stirred tank is modelled as mixed flow with explicit G–L–S resistances, not as a pseudo-homogeneous bed.

Problem 16.9 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.9Rate and model for diesel hydrodesulfurization

Sulfur content in diesel oil can be reduced by hydrodesulfurization reaction using cobalt molybdenum catalyst. Hydrogen gas is fed into the reactor and reacts with sulfur compound in diesel. The reaction product is hydrogen sulfide and hydrocarbon without sulfur. The reaction is normally operated at 20-30 bar and 250-300°C. Diesel remains in liquid phase and hydrogen is in gas phase. To ensure that most of sulfur reacts, an excess amount of hydrogen is fed into the rector.

(a) The overall rate of reaction can be written as $-r_{H_2}=k_{vg}C_{H_2(g)}$
(b) The overall rate of reaction can also be written as $-r_{sulfur}=k_{vl}C_{sulfur}$
(c) If first-order reaction is assumed in dissolved hydrogen gas and in sulfur compound, the overall rate of reaction can be written as $-r_{H_2}=\eta kC_{H_2}C_{sulfur}$, where $C_{H_2}$ and $C_{sulfur}$ are concentration of each component adsorbed on the catalyst surface.
(d) The reactor model can be written as $u\dfrac{dC}{dz}+(1-\varepsilon_B)\rho_{cat}\eta r=0$

Source slide 114. Decide which statement does not hold.

Problem 16.9 · solution

PROBLEM 16.9(a) fails: with H₂ in excess the rate follows the sulfur compound

  • (a) does not hold: excess H₂ means its concentration hardly changes, so the overall rate cannot be first order in gas-phase H₂.
  • (b) holds: B-limiting case of 16-6, $r'=k'_{app}C_{Blb}$, here written per volume.
  • (c) holds as the intrinsic rate at surface concentrations, with $\eta$ for pore diffusion.
  • (d) holds: the steady 1-D plug flow balance of 16-7, consumption rate $r$.

Problem 16.10 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 16.10How many beds, and which quench?

A gas-oil hydrotreater receives feed at 350 °C. If all the catalyst were in one adiabatic bed, the outlet would reach 440 °C. The catalyst must stay below 410 °C.

(a) Equal beds are used, with quench back to 350 °C between them. How many beds are needed, and what is the peak temperature?

(b) The recycle compressor has spare capacity and the H₂S level in the reactor is high. Which quench fluid would you choose, and why?

$T_{in}$350 °C
One-bed outlet440 °C
Limit410 °C

New problem for this lecture, built on Ancheyta, Ch. 3.

Problem 16.10 · solution

PROBLEM 16.10Two beds, peak 395 °C; quench with hydrogen

Equal beds, quench to the inlet$N\ge\dfrac{\Delta T_{ad}}{T_{max}-T_{in}}$, $\ T_{peak}=T_{in}+\dfrac{\Delta T_{ad}}{N}$
$\Delta T_{ad}=440-350=90$ K; allowed rise $410-350=60$ K
limit per bed
$N\ge90/60=1.5\ \Rightarrow\ N=2$; rise $45$ K; peak $395$ °C
equal beds, one quench zone
(b) H₂ quench: compressor available; dilutes H₂S, an HDS inhibitor; replenishes H₂
Ancheyta, Table 3.2

Lecture 16

Key Takeaways

1

Choose a trickle bed for three phases and a long-lived catalyst; keep it in trickle flow and spread the liquid evenly.

2

Compute $\Delta P_L$, $\Delta P_G$ with Ergun, then $\chi$ gives the two-phase drop and the liquid saturation.

3

Add the resistances in series and find the largest; know whether gas or liquid limits before judging wetting.

4

Start from 1-D plug flow; check Mears with the real $Bo$ before trusting a lab bed.

5

Scale at equal mass fluxes, not equal LHSV; manage hydrotreater heat with beds and quench.

Before you leave
